76 years of post-midterm CPI data says tomorrow is a small green day. 2022 says otherwise 

Since closing under 7400 on Friday, the S&P 500 has rallied over 170 points, pushing us back to 7550 after Thursday’s 4.4% flush. October CPI hits at 8:30 AM ET tomorrow, the first print since the midterms. I went back through all 19 post-midterm CPI prints since 1950 to see how $SPX closed that day.

I like to approach things systematically, so here are three potential scenarios I’m watching for tomorrow:

Scenario 1: Bullish
This has happened 11 of 19 times. The average gain is +0.90%, which puts $SPX right around 7620. Take out 2022’s +5.54% and the other 10 averaged +0.44%, which lands us around 7580. If the post-print move holds 7580, the bounce stays alive and 7620 is next.

Scenario 2: Bearish
This has happened 6 of 19 times. The average loss is -0.98%, which puts $SPX just under 7500. The worst was 1958 at -1.94%, which would take us toward 7400. We lose 7550 early, 7500 doesn’t hold, and Friday’s 7376 close comes back into play.

Scenario 3: Neutral
This has happened 2 of 19 times. 1990 closed +0.03% and 2010 closed +0.02%, both inside a tenth of a percent. The print lands in line, we chop around 7550 and the market waits for the next catalyst.

Across 19 midterms, the post-CPI move has been green more often than red. Pair that with last week’s heavy selloff into support and a continuation move looks more likely.

Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., during the Nvidia GTC conference in San Jose, California, US, on Wednesday, March 18, 2026.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's admission of an affair with a purported Chinese spy has raised questions about his future at the company, and what happens if the 63-year-old co-founder, who built the chipmaker into one of the most valuable businesses on the planet, is forced out.

Shares of Nvidia sank more than 5% on Monday, even as the broader market rallied sharply, after Huang acknowledged the affair in a message to staff on Sunday, and said that the board was launching an investigation into whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence agency. The board said it has "confidence in Jensen," and that it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised."

The New York Times first reported that the Chinese businesswoman was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, according to people briefed on the intelligence circulated in a memo among the Trump administration in the spring. China has called the allegation a smear.

While Nvidia says Huang will continue to lead the company during the probe, pressure is rapidly mounting on the chipmaker, whose technology has powered the first four years of the generative artificial intelligence boom. Leaders from both parties are calling for briefings, and Democrats poised to take control of both houses of Congress are calling for investigations and new legislation "to stop advanced AI chips from fueling China's military," Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts wrote in a post on X on Monday.

Huang has outsized influence over Nvidia, and is the sole face of the company with no clear second-in-command. He's also among the loudest champions of AI in the country, is critical to the financing of the broader infrastructure buildout and has a close relationship with President Donald Trump, giving Nvidia a front-row seat when it comes to discussions on AI policy, safety and regulation.

"The issue at Nvidia is that there is no clear successor to Jensen, and we had expected him to stay in this role for at least 10 more years," analysts at Melius Research said in a Monday research note.

Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at Bernstein, told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Monday that, "Jensen is Nvidia. Nvidia is Jensen." He added that Huang "runs the thing pretty much top down," and "sort of pulls all the strings."

Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Nvidia has long maintained a flat, non-hierarchical organizational structure. Huang has deep involvement in the company's day-to-day operations, with around 60 direct reports, and frequently serves as its spokesperson in front of world leaders and at industry conferences. In addition to being co-founder and CEO, Huang is also Nvidia's president.

geek alert....

there's "vol", "vol of vol"...and dare I say it..."vol of vol of vol"... good god.  In simpler terms: "the variability of implied vol on VIX options" ...that's vol of vol of vol.

and by at least one count, this has reached a record...below, the 1m realized vol of the VVIX. higher than Volmaggedon, the Covid Crash, the Aug'24 VIX event, the Tariff Tantrum.

In the last month, the $VVIX has had up moves of 18.7%, 14.2% and 49.3% (Thursday, 11/5). It also had a 15.8% down day (11/4).  the surge last Thursday drives a tremendous proportion of the overall 1m realized vol. when it comes to vol, "big moves matter most."

in markets, p/l is about prices. we talk about vol only because it can be a shorthand for prices. if you move the implied vol (VVIX) on a 1m $VIX straddle up by 20%, you move the straddle price up by the same amount. if you move the implied vol input down by 20%, the straddle price declines by 20%.

The market has been broken since July, and despite this morning's bounce, I see little reason to believe the correction is over.

Failed breakouts, deteriorating leadership, and stocks trading below their 8/21-day moving averages have made this an extremely difficult environment.

That's why we've been mostly in CASH. Some traders are taking tactical positions, but I'd rather take a few small paper cuts than suffer massive drawdowns.

Plenty of investors have watched individual stocks lose 50% or more while waiting for a recovery that never came.

*

Now we have another complication: $NVDA.

Over the weekend, unverified allegations involving Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy circulated, raising concerns about whether #Nvidia could trigger another market selloff.

But so far, the broader market is largely ignoring the headlines. $SPY is up, $QQQ is up, while $NVDA is down approximately 5%.

That divergence is worth watching.

*

Nvidia's technical picture is terrible. Remember that failed breakout? It was one of the worst we've seen.

Since then, the stock has remained below its moving averages, with rallies offering better shorting opportunities than sustainable long entries.

Now #NVDA has broken below $181.46 and is trading near its yearly lows. The next major downside reference is in the $160s.

With the controversy, significant gaps, and ongoing selling pressure, there may be much easier stocks to trade. You don't have to catch every falling knife.

*

$QQQ has been leading this correction lower. The warning signs appeared back on October 6 with a topping tail, followed by a failed breakout, a break below the 8-day moving average, and an unfilled downside gap.

$QQQ eventually reached $647.

Now we're seeing a modest bounce, but $664, Friday's high, is the first important resistance level. A rally toward that area could offer another opportunity to establish shorts rather than chase the upside.

*
$SPY recently tested its 200-day moving average around $732 after falling roughly 6% from its highs.
We're now near $740, with Friday's high at $742 acting as immediate resistance.

If $SPY clears $742, there's room for a move toward $750. But if it gets rejected and forms another bear flag, the next test of the 200-day moving average could be trouble.

*

BLOOD IN THE STREET ACCOUNT UPDATE

Despite my defensive trading stance, I finally put 25% of my Blood in the Street Account to work on Thursday.

This strategy has a specific process: the S&P 500 must decline at least 5% from its highs before capital gets deployed into an S&P 500-correlated large-cap fund.

It's not about buying $QQQ, $IWM, or individual stocks.

The strategy has worked 18 out of 18 times historically, and with the S&P down approximately 6%, the rules triggered another purchase.

*

So, I'm still mostly in cash tactically, but selectively putting longer-term capital to work.

This market remains broken. Don't confuse an oversold bounce with a confirmed recovery.

Protect your capital, respect your levels, and stay patient. There will be better opportunities ahead.

Does open-source code make decentralized systems more secure?

Stacks co-founder Muneeb Ali says transparent systems may be clunkier early on, but they harden faster with every attack

"There are two models out there. One is that your code is fully open source. It's out in the wild. Imagine Bitcoin itself, or some DEXs that are open source. Anyone can verify how it's working, they can view it, and if there's a bug, they can come and exploit it."

"And then the other side is you have the black box exchanges. They have the advantage, in a way, that you can't really see exactly what they're doing, but you're still trying to poke from the outside to see if there's anything you can find that you can exploit."

"My view has been that the first model is sometimes more clunky early on, but it gets hardened faster. Eventually, everyone in the world has taken their shot to see if there's anything here."

"So I think over a long enough timeline, the decentralized versions actually become more secure, just because they've had more eyes on them, and they're hardened in a harsher environment."

posts.name: Captain Eli
posts.text:
In February 2004 Elon Musk wrote the check that put Tesla Motors on the road: $6.5 million of a $7.5 million Series A, plus the chairman's seat.

He led the next round in February 2005. He co-led the $40 million round in May 2006 that brought in Larry Page and Sergey Brin. That August he published The Secret Tesla Motors Master Plan on the company blog, a sports car to pay for an affordable car, and so on down to the mass market. He pushed for the Roadster's carbon fiber body. By January 2009, Bloomberg reported, he had put $70 million of his own money into the company.

CNBC still wrote this on September 10, 2018: "Though Musk didn't found Tesla, his DNA is very much a part of the company."

Read the very next sentence of the same article: "He was one of its original investors and chairman of the board in 2004 before becoming CEO in 2008."

Original investor. Chairman in 2004. CNBC typed both facts and still filed him under "didn't found."

That question had been settled nine years earlier, in court and in writing. In 2009 Martin Eberhard sued, and one of the things he asked a San Mateo County judge for was a declaration that he and Marc Tarpenning were the only two founders. In July the judge struck that request. In September the case was settled and Tesla named five co-founders: Eberhard, Tarpenning, Elon Musk, JB Straubel and Ian Wright.

Eberhard's own statement that day: "As a co-founder of the company, Elon's contributions to Tesla have been extraordinary."

The man who went to court over the title called Elon Musk a co-founder in his own words. A business network still decided it knew better.

Elon Musk has told his side too. In April 2022 he wrote that the Tesla he walked into was "a shell corp" with "literally nothing but a biz plan to commercialize AC Propulsion's Tzero car, which was introduced to me by JB Straubel, *not* Eberhard." Then: "If filing a shell corp constitutes 'founding a company', then I'd be the only founder of PayPal, since I filed the original incorporation docs for http://X.com (later renamed PayPal), but that's not what founding means."

And the line that says the most: "I put in all I had, whereas Eberhard, who was worth over $10M at the time, refused to invest a penny to help Tesla."

So why slip a false founder line into a 2018 piece? Look at the headline it sat under: "Musk's defiant, rebel CEO persona is putting his company and its investors at risk, say management experts." The article argued Tesla needed "someone to help keep Musk in line." Shrink his role at the birth of the company and it gets much easier to argue he is replaceable at the top of it. Legacy media has been running that play on Elon Musk for years.

Tesla closed at $19.03 a share, split-adjusted, the day that story ran. On November 9, 2026 it closed at $378.05. The investors CNBC's experts were so worried about made nearly twenty times their money by keeping him exactly where he was.

posts.text:
Something that merits more discussion amongst those who believe it was a mistake by both the Biden and Trump administrations to allow the export of less powerful GPUs to China:

Since the summer of 2025, it has increasingly been *China*, not just DC, blocking Nvidia GPUs in China. Within weeks of Secretary Lutnick saying the goal was to get Chinese developers "addicted" to the American technology stack, Beijing began pressuring its tech giants to stop buying the H20. Then it ordered them to stop buying the RTX Pro 6000D, sent customs teams to the ports to crack down on Nvidia chip imports, and barred foreign AI chips from new state-funded data centers. And as of last week, Reuters reports that roughly 600,000 H200s are sitting in Hong Kong because Beijing won't approve large-scale imports of a chip that is still better than anything China's own industry makes at scale.

If allowing the export of these less powerful GPUs was a policy mistake that *advantaged* China, then why is *China* the one blocking them?

From my perspective, China understands that if they are dependent on American AI hardware - either on the ground in China or accessed remotely via the wide range of southeast Asian clouds (which include SE Asian availability zones from the largest American hyperscalers) - then we have immense leverage over them in any future conflict. Being able to turn off the clouds instantly is actually the greatest leverage.

Yes, Chinese AI labs still want Nvidia chips. Gray market prices for H200 servers have roughly tripled over the past year. But that is exactly the point. Beijing is willing to impose real costs on its own AI labs to avoid dependence on American GPUs, which tells you how Beijing views GPU imports: not as a gift, but as a threat to its own ambitions.

Maybe, just maybe, selling China GPUs that trail our own state of the art, so that Chinese developers stay “addicted” to American GPUs and China doesn't build an alternative AI hardware ecosystem that we have no control or influence over *and* that China could share over time with our adversaries, was actually a smart, pro-American national defense policy. And letting them access southeast Asian clouds might be an even smarter policy as so easy to turn clouds off.

I believed and still believed it was smart policy. And I say this as someone whose posts here are hawkish enough on China that I won't travel there anymore.

And note that both the Biden and Trump administration allowed the export of less powerful GPUs to China for all of these reasons. It was only under the Trump administration that China woke up to the risk of what was actually a pretty smart, pro-national defense policy and then China began restricting GPUs.

The lesson of the H20 is that a deliberately crippled chip doesn't keep China on our stack. Beijing moved against the H20 and RTX Pro 6000D as it concluded that domestic Chinese chips had caught up to them. So if China develops an alternative AI hardware ecosystem that it shares with Russia, Iran and North Korea, we will look back and think it would have been even smarter to offer China the B30A in 2025 instead of the H200s we eventually approved case-by-case. Especially given the H200 is not the frontier: with Vera Rubin now in full production, it is two generations behind what American labs are buying.

All of this is to say that Jensen has been consistently lobbying for a position that was adapted by both the Biden *and* Trump admins *and* looks smarter every month that goes by as Chinese labs increasingly adapt their MoE architectures to domestic Chinese hardware. DeepSeek reportedly gave Huawei and Cambricon early access to V4 instead of Nvidia and AMD, and a Huawei-led team has since post-trained V4-Pro on Ascend chips.

And if America *ever* falls behind China in AI, the China hawks here in America who helped accelerate the creation of this alternative Chinese AI hardware ecosystem will deserve a significant share of the blame.

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
This can only be settled in the streets. Nick gets to fight with a calculator though because Corey’s endurance is obviously unfair.

In all seriousness, I think this debate is built on a false premise. There’s no such thing as “passive” investing. Everyone deviates from the global market cap portfolio. The S&P 500 is a committee-picked large cap US stock fund. Choosing it is an active decision. Your stock/bond mix is an active decision. Rebalancing is an active decision. Blah blah blah. You prob know my rant by now.

So the real question isn’t active vs. passive. It’s low fee, low turnover and rules-based vs. high fee, high turnover and discretionary. And then whether any of it actually fits the investor’s planning needs.

There are silly index funds and very good ones. SPY is a great one IMO. It’s cheap, diversified and lets winners run while losers shrink. It doesn’t so much distort prices as accept the prices set by more active investors at the margin. And there are lots of great active deviations from it too. Indexing isn’t the end all be all, especially now that you can run a smart active strategy in an ETF for close to index fund fees.

Aggregate bond index funds are a great example of a flawed methodology, yet people revere them for no real reason other than cheap diversification. They’re weighted by how much debt issuers sell, so the biggest borrowers get the biggest weights. Their duration drifts based on what the Treasury and corporations decide to issue, not on anything the investor needs. And because bonds trade far less than stocks, index rules matter more. Look at the forced selling when bonds get downgraded out of investment grade indexes. They borrow market cap logic from stocks, where it makes sense, and apply it to debt, where it doesn’t. That can distort prices and serves the end investor poorly.

Funny thing is the critics usually aim at the wrong target. Broad equity index funds are generally great. It’s the bond indexes that make less sense. So Nick is right that equity indexing is a huge win for investors, and Corey is right that index methodology can distort prices. They’re just talking past each other in a debate that’s a lot more nuanced than either side admits.

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
Not really. You get a small cushion, not protection.

The only buffer is the option premium you collect, roughly 1% a month. In a real selloff that barely dents the loss. In the 2025 drawdown, QQQ fell about 23% and QQQI fell 20%. In the current pullback since the October peak, it's roughly 14% versus 12%. So you're eating about 80% of the downside.

This is a structural problem. Stocks go up more often than they go down, so a strategy that trims both sides evenly will lag over time. It's basically a lower beta Nasdaq that charges you 0.68% to be one. You're not getting safety and income. You're paying more for lower beta.

posts.text:
The math is fine. The accounting is wrong.

When a fund pays out 11%, its price drops by that amount. That's not income. It's a withdrawal with less control over taxes and timing than selling shares yourself.

What matters is total return. If the fund earns 6% and pays 11%, you're eating 5% of your principal every year. The "paycheck" shrinks each year and inflation and taxes make it worse. Those yields usually come from covered calls or return of capital, which cap your upside and leave you with the downside. 

Take the popular "distribution Yield" funds for example. QQQI sells call options on the Nasdaq 100. That premium is the "income," but it means handing someone else your gains above a certain level. You keep the downside and give up part of the upside thinking you got safer "income" when you actually locked in a lower total return. 

And the upside is where stock returns come from, usually in a few sharp rallies after selloffs. In April 2026 alone, QQQ returned about 15.7% to QQQI's 10.3%. Add a 0.68% fee versus 0.18% for QQQ and it falls further behind. It wins in flat markets, but the longer you hold the longer you give up the compound upside trend. 

Here's the actual "paycheck" result using the OP example. Both accounts paid out the exact same paychecks on the exact same days. The one that "sold shares" just has more left because it didn't pay the high fees or cap its upside with covered call "income".

That's perfect actually. All of MMT starts with the assumption "first, assume a jet just exists..." Reminds me of the old economics can opener joke...

The accounting nets out the same, but the sequence starts in the private sector. The government can only buy the jet because a private firm built it. 

Banks lend, firms invest and households spend without the Treasury ever entering the picture. Government spending is a claim on that private output, not the thing that creates it. It sets the rules and acts as a backstop in crises, but it's a referee, not the engine.

Somebody had to build the jet first and most of the resources in our economy are built with the support of private borrowing that doesn't require reserves or govt spending first.
